prize_parts.citation: for methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which transformed empirical industrial organization and the analysis of market power

statement.case_for: The random-coefficients demand framework with endogenous prices (Berry 1994; Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995) and the dynamic-industry models built on it are among the most widely adopted empirical toolkits in economics. They are used in merger review, antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental analysis. The core work is about thirty years old, so it has been tested, replicated, criticised and refined in a very large number of applications. That is the kind of confirmation I weight most heavily as someone who works on reliability of findings. The known weaknesses, such as numerical sensitivity of the estimators and weak identification, are documented in the literature and have largely been addressed with better algorithms and diagnostics. This is not a fragile result that depends on a single data set or lab. The attribution is also comparatively clean for a field this large. BLP is a named three-author contribution, and Pakes additionally anchors the dynamic-games strand, so a three-person prize tracks the credit well. All ten members who ranked B001 placed it in their top three, and I take that as agreement across fields on breadth and durability. I do not treat the count as evidence of merit in itself.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is chiefly a methodological toolkit, and some colleagues may prefer prizes for substantive discoveries. Credit also spans three strands (demand estimation, production-function and dynamic-game methods, and the earlier new empirical IO programme), and a three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, whose claims are real. In applied work the results of structural IO can be sensitive to functional-form and instrument choices. I rely on background knowledge for adoption and sensitivity claims and have not verified citation counts independently.

responses.point: Krusell proposes Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan for B001 and argues that Bresnahan's role in the new empirical IO and early differentiated-product demand estimation could reasonably displace Levinsohn.
responses.response: I agree this is the most serious attribution question on B001 and that Bresnahan's contribution to the empirical IO agenda is large. I still prefer Levinsohn in the third slot because the citation I propose is about estimating demand with endogenous prices and equilibrium supply. That is the specific content of the 1995 paper, and Levinsohn is its co-author. Bresnahan's strongest claim is to the broader programme and to earlier demand and market-power work. That could support a different or wider citation, but it would make the prize less tightly tied to one identifiable method. I would keep the point open if colleagues think the programme-level framing is better than the method-level one. I also note that Krusell keeps B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore, which is a cleaner attribution than the three-name version on the ballot.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B002 first because collateral constraints and the financial accelerator are conceptually deep and general, and shaped post-2008 research and policy. He also flags that the 2022 prize and the Gertler versus Gilchrist choice complicate the case.
responses.response: I agree that the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is deep and I ranked B002 third. My hesitation is the empirical side. Identifying the amplification channel from data is model-dependent and harder than the theory suggests. By contrast, BLP-type methods have been stress-tested directly, including on whether the estimators converge and which instruments are credible. The overlap with Bernanke's 2022 prize makes B002 more awkward on novelty, and adding Gertler is an attribution problem rather than a clean extension. I would support B002 as a strong alternative, probably with Kiyotaki and Moore alone, but I do not think it should come ahead of B001 on current evidence.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B013 first. She argues that the task framework and the trade-shock evidence combine new data, credible identification and a conceptual framework. She treats the exclusion of Dorn under the three-name cap as a close call.
responses.response: I ranked B013 second and I share the view that it is a major empirical contribution with real policy influence. The China-shock results have been replicated and extended. My reservation is that the magnitude and persistence of the local labour-market effects and the identification strategy are still debated. The credit is also split across two strands, with the task framework drawing on authors outside the ballot and the Katz-Goldin lineage overlapping with recent recognition. Dorn's exclusion is a real cost. In my own opening proposal I named Autor, Hanson and Dorn on the strength of the China-shock work, while Enflo's trio keeps Katz for the skill-demand strand. That difference shows the attribution is less settled than for B001. I would keep B013 as the leading alternative and would not object to it as a later prize.

uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan or Levinsohn should take the third slot, and whether the committee wants a method-level or programme-level citation.
Whether the committee gives a methods-and-tools contribution the same weight as a substantive empirical discovery.
How far the known numerical and identification sensitivities of BLP-type estimators affect confidence in applied results, which I assess from background knowledge only.
Whether the 2022 prize reduces room for B002 and whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be credited if B002 advances.
Whether the long-run robustness of the China-shock magnitudes is settled enough for B013.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the B001 credited names appear among my listed co-authors or institutional ties. Some of my frequent co-authors (for example Camerer) and my Harvard evolutionary-dynamics network are not credited on B001, B013 or B002. My metascience orientation is a perspective on how I weigh replication and robustness, not a personal connection.
